strengths: Clear and well-motivated observation: user-oriented (iterative) optimization pairs in PIE bias fine-tuning toward local edits, and restructuring pairs across different users for the same problem (PIE-Problem) exposes global algorithmic innovations; the motivating examples in Figures 2 and 8-10 are informative.

Comprehensive experimental setup: multiple models (CodeLlama 7B/13B/34B, DeepSeek-Coder 7B/33B, GPT-3.5/GPT-4), BEST@1 and BEST@8 decoding, deterministic timing via gem5, and released dataset/code/evaluation scripts supporting reproducibility.

Thorough analysis beyond the headline results: optimization-type classification (GPT-4 + human audit), correctness bottleneck analysis, comparison against self-correction and curriculum-learning baselines, merge-weight (lambda) sensitivity analysis, and a quantitative error analysis (Table 4).
The correctness-vs-aggressiveness framing (PIE-User too conservative, PIE-Problem too aggressive) is a useful empirical insight, and model merging as a remedy is intuitive and empirically supported.
weaknesses: The core contribution is conceptually simple: the 'problem-oriented' dataset is a re-pairing of the existing PIE data by problem rather than by user, filtered at >90% speedup. The novelty is limited to dataset curation plus applying existing model merging techniques.

Key comparisons are not fully controlled: PIE-User fine-tuning uses performance-conditioned generation while PIE-Problem uses a simple instruction. Some of the reported gains could stem from the instruction format rather than the pair construction itself; an ablation isolating this factor is missing.

The PIE-Problem training distribution is restricted to pairs with >90% relative speedup, while evaluation is on the original PIE test set. This distribution shift could inflate %OPT/SPEEDUP in a way that does not reflect better general optimization ability; the paper does not analyze this confound.

Correctness drops substantially under PIE-Problem fine-tuning (e.g., 13-13.5% Correct for CodeLlama 34B vs 36.57% under PIE-User), and the final merged-model numbers come at the cost of a brittle, tuning-sensitive merge procedure (performance depends on a narrow lambda range); robustness across a second benchmark is not demonstrated.
Evaluation is confined to the PIE/CodeNet ecosystem; no external benchmark of code optimization is used, so the significance of the improvements to broader code-optimization settings is unclear.
The optimization-type analysis relies on only 100 human-annotated pairs and GPT-4 judgments on 1,000 pairs, which is thin support for a central motivating claim.

Writing quality issues (e.g., 'Tale 2', 't is important to note', grammatical slips) and some presentation looseness reduce polish; several justifications (e.g., the 90% threshold citing a 2012 blog post) are not rigorous.

strengths: The core observation — that PIE pairs built from a single programmer's iterative submissions bias models toward local, incremental edits — is intuitive and well-motivated, and the worked examples (Figures 2, 8-10) illustrate it convincingly.
Releasing the reconstructed PIE-Problem dataset, code, and evaluation scripts supports reproducibility, and the use of gem5 simulation for deterministic latency measurement is a methodological plus.

The experiments span two model families at several scales, include prompt-only baselines (instruct, CoT), and the reported gains (e.g., 51.76% -> 76.65% %OPT, 2.65x -> 5.09x speedup under BEST@8) are substantial in absolute terms.
The paper identifies the correctness bottleneck under PIE-Problem fine-tuning and includes an error analysis (Table 4) and merge-weight sensitivity study (Figure 5), which add interpretive value.
weaknesses: A critical confound undermines the central claim: PIE-Problem pairs are filtered by a >=90% relative speedup threshold while PIE-User pairs use a >=10% threshold, and the training sets differ substantially in size (14,051 vs 56,086 pairs). The observed gains may therefore reflect the speedup distribution of the target solutions rather than 'cross-programmer algorithmic innovation.' The decisive ablation is missing: fine-tuning on user-oriented pairs filtered at the same >=90% threshold to isolate the effect of cross-user pair construction. Without it, the headline claim is not cleanly supported.

The definition of 'problem-oriented' pairs is purely speed-based; whether a pair embodies a 'global algorithmic optimization' is only verified post hoc via GPT-4 classification on 1,000 sampled pairs (with human verification on only 100). The paper itself notes GPT-4 systematically over-labels 'global,' weakening the dataset-analysis evidence.

The model merging contribution is incremental: linear interpolation and SLERP are well-established techniques, and the most natural baseline — simply fine-tuning on the union of PIE-User and PIE-Problem, or mixing datasets in training — is conspicuously absent. It is unclear merging beats joint training.

The correctness drop under PIE-Problem fine-tuning (e.g., 37.41% vs 59.49% Correct for DeepSeek-Coder 33B at BEST@1) is severe and suggests the model may largely be imitating fast solutions rather than performing semantics-aware optimization; the analysis of this phenomenon remains shallow.

The 90% threshold rationale rests on a blog post citation (Atwood, 2012), and 'for the first time propose a problem-oriented perspective' overstates the novelty of what is essentially a re-filtering/re-pairing of an existing dataset.
No statistical significance testing or variance reporting across sampling runs; BEST@8 improvements partly reflect best-of-n selection effects that are not dissected.

Writing quality is below the bar for a top venue: typos ('Tale 2', 't is important to note', 'the optimization ratio of from 51.76%'), informal phrasing ('the simpler the better'), and a thin related-work section that omits recent LLM-based program optimization efforts.
The merged model is never evaluated outside the optimization task, so the claim that merging 'retains the original capabilities' is unsupported.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated reframing of the code optimization problem: shifting from user-oriented (same programmer, iterative submissions) to problem-oriented (cross-programmer) optimization pairs is an intuitive insight supported by concrete qualitative examples (Figures 2, 8-10) and a statistical analysis of optimization types (Figure 3).

Solid and careful experimental infrastructure: deterministic gem5 CPU simulation for timing, unified compilation settings (GCC 9.4.0, -O3, C++17), unit-test-based correctness checking, and the established %OPT / SPEEDUP / Correct metrics from the PIE work, which makes results reproducible and comparable.

Broad empirical coverage: multiple Code LLMs (CodeLlama 7B/13B/34B, DeepSeek-Coder 7B/33B) across parameter scales, comparisons against instruct/CoT prompting of GPT-3.5/GPT-4, and BEST@1/BEST@8 decoding, showing consistent gains for the problem-oriented setting.

Thoughtful analysis beyond the headline numbers: identification of the correctness bottleneck under PIE-Problem fine-tuning, ablation over merge weights (Figure 5), comparisons against Self-Correct and curriculum-learning baselines, and a useful error breakdown (Table 4) that points to future directions.
Good faith release of the dataset, code, and evaluation scripts, supporting reproducibility and follow-up work.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core contribution is a dataset curation change (re-pairing solutions from different users above a 90% speedup threshold) plus standard weight-space model merging (linear interpolation, SLERP); neither technique is technically new, so the paper's impact rests mainly on the empirical insight.

Potential confound in the main comparison: PIE-Problem pairs require >90% relative speedup, meaning fine-tuning targets are systematically much faster programs. The observed gains may partly reflect the model imitating an inherently faster solution distribution rather than learning 'global algorithmic innovation'. No control experiment (e.g., PIE-User pairs filtered by the same 90% threshold) isolates the effect of the cross-user perspective itself.

Unfair/uneven comparison setup: PIE-User fine-tuning uses performance-conditioned generation prompts while PIE-Problem uses a simple instruction ('the simpler the better'), so the two fine-tuning regimes differ in both data and prompting; the headline 51.76% → 76.65% improvement is therefore not a clean ablation.
The 90% threshold is justified only by a citation to a blog post (Atwood, 2012); no sensitivity analysis of this design choice is provided, though it fundamentally shapes the dataset.

BEST@k selection uses test-set correctness and timing to pick the best candidate, which is a strong oracle at inference time; the practicality of this assumption is not discussed, and statistical significance/standard deviations are not reported.

Some claims are speculative and under-supported, e.g., explanations for why curriculum learning fails or why DeepSeek-Coder 7B beats CodeLlama 34B are post-hoc speculation without targeted experiments.

Writing quality issues: typos ('Tale 2', 't is important to note'), some imprecise statements, and the possibility that CodeLlama/DeepSeek pretraining corpora already contain competitive-programming solutions from CodeNet-like sources is not addressed, which threatens the validity of 'unseen' test problems.

The model merging solution is somewhat ad hoc: it interpolates two LoRA fine-tunes of the same base model, and while effective, no theory or deeper analysis is offered for why merging resolves the correctness-speedup trade-off.

strengths: The problem-oriented perspective for constructing code optimization pairs is a simple yet effective reframing of the PIE dataset, and the paper supports the claim that it captures more 'global algorithmic' optimizations with a credible multi-dimensional analysis (Graph Edit Distance on CFGs, semantic embeddings with t-SNE, and human+LLM classification of 100/1000 sampled pairs).

The main fine-tuning results (Table 1) are convincing: consistent improvements in %OPT, SPEEDUP, and CORRECT across four LLM families and multiple parameter scales (e.g., 31.24%→58.89% %OPT for Qwen2.5-Coder 32B), which rules out the gains being a single-model artifact.

The anchor verification mechanism is well-motivated and clearly distinct from prior test-generation feedback methods: using the guaranteed-correct 'slow code' as an execution oracle avoids the error-prone synthetic test-case labels used in code generation. The comparison against Self-Debugging and Direct Test Generation (Tables 2 and 4) across three LLM backbones is an appropriate baseline design, and the supplementary PIE-baseline experiments and three detailed case studies strengthen the analysis.

Useful ablations: the PCO percentage analysis (Fig. 5) shows data efficiency of the new perspective, and the training/implementation details in the appendix (LoRA config, prompts, gem5 setup, GCC flags) plus the stated public code release support reproducibility.
The 'optimization tax' observation is a genuine and practically important phenomenon in code optimization that the paper identifies and addresses rather than ignoring.
weaknesses: The core contribution is conceptually simple: re-pairing submissions across users sorted by runtime is essentially a dataset curation trick on top of PIE. While effective, the intellectual novelty is limited, and the 'Extra Quantity Bonus' (the combinatorial scaling argument) is not actually leveraged since the experiments fix the number of pairs at 78K for fairness.

Potential confound in the PCO construction: pairs are selected by 'top speedup rankings' for each problem. This biases PCO toward pairs with extreme runtime differences, which may itself inflate measured SPEEDUP and %OPT gains on the test set (which is also constructed in the problem-oriented manner), independent of any benefit from algorithmic diversity. A control selecting pairs by other criteria (e.g., random pairings across users, or matched speedups) is missing.

The evaluation test set is small: only 41 unique problems and 978 pairs. Several of the reported deltas (e.g., a few points of CORRECT) could be sensitive to this limited problem diversity, and no statistical significance testing or variance analysis (over random seeds or sampling) is provided.

Anchor verification has notable practical limitations that are under-discussed: (1) correctness is judged against only ~3 LLM-generated test inputs, so 'CORRECT' likely overstates true functional equivalence; (2) for large inputs the slow code may time out, restricting usable test cases; (3) refinement uses a maximum of 1 iteration and is only evaluated at BEST@1, leaving the behavior at higher iteration counts unexplored.

Some findings are thin: Finding 1 and Finding 2 are accompanied by plausible but unverified post-hoc explanations, and the instruct/CoT prompting results mainly show prompting fails, which slightly narrows the paper's practical takeaway to fine-tuning + refinement.

Writing quality issues: minor grammatical errors throughout, some redundancy between Sections 3/4 and the appendix, and Fig. 3 (t-SNE scatter) provides weak quantitative evidence for the semantic-diversity claim.

strengths: The problem-oriented dataset construction (PCO) is simple, practical, and well-motivated: pairing submissions across programmers by runtime plausibly exposes more diverse, algorithm-level optimizations than per-user iterative pairs, and the paper supports this with multiple analyses (CFG edit distance, semantic embeddings, and human/GPT-4 categorization of optimization types).

The evaluation is reasonably broad: five code LLMs across scales, both prompting (instruction, CoT) and fine-tuning settings, BEST@1 and BEST@8 decoding, gem5-based runtime measurement on top of -O3 compilation, and a data-efficiency analysis (Fig. 5).

The anchor verification framework is a sensible use of a property unique to optimization (the slow code is a correct oracle), and it is compared against two relevant baselines (self-debugging, direct test generation) across three strong backbones.
Case studies and qualitative examples (Appendix H, I) effectively illustrate the incremental vs. global optimization distinction, and the paper is generally well written and easy to follow.
weaknesses: A central confound undermines the main claim: PCO pairs are constructed not just by 'problem-oriented' reordering but by selecting the top-speedup-ranked pairs for each problem (Sec. 3.2). The reported gains (%OPT 31.24%→58.89%, speedup 2.95×→5.22×) may therefore reflect training on speedup-biased targets rather than any benefit from integrating diverse programmers' ideas. No ablation disentangles the reordering itself from the speedup-based selection (e.g., a random-pair cross-user baseline, or PIE pairs reselected by speedup).

Limited conceptual novelty. PCO is essentially a data-curation variant (sorting by runtime instead of by user), and anchor verification is a straightforward instantiation of execution-feedback self-repair where test outputs come from the slow code instead of an LLM. Both ideas are incremental relative to PIE (Shypula et al., 2024) and existing test-based refinement work (CodeT, Self-Debugging, LDB), which the paper acknowledges as baselines rather than cites as direct precedents for the verification mechanism.

Correctness assessment in the refinement stage relies on only 3 LLM-generated test inputs (App. F) executed through the slow code. This is a very weak oracle; many incorrect programs would pass these few cases, and the reported CORRECT numbers (and hence the claimed 'optimization tax' mitigation) could be significantly inflated. Test-case coverage is not analyzed.

The test set is small (41 unique problems, 978 pairs per Table 3), and no statistical significance, variance across seeds, or confidence intervals are reported for the headline differences, despite fine-tuning with LoRA at only 2 epochs where run-to-run variance can be non-trivial.

Evaluation is confined to competitive-programming C++ programs from CodeNet with a single metric family (runtime); the limitation section admits memory and other dimensions are ignored, and the practical applicability of gem5-simulated competitive-programming speedups to real-world software optimization is questionable.

Some inconsistencies weaken confidence: minor discrepancies in reported numbers across abstract/intro/body (e.g., 58.89% vs 58.90%), and the analysis in Appendix B notes GPT-4 systematically misclassifies 'global' optimizations, yet the headline claim of 'global algorithmic' richness in PCO leans partly on such LLM-based categorization.

The finding that CORRECT declines under BEST@8 for PCO (Finding 1) is noted but not investigated; the interpretation of Finding 2 (%OPT≈CORRECT) is superficial and does not lead to a methodological improvement beyond anchor verification.

Comparison fairness in Table 2: anchor verification uses GPT-4o/DeepSeek-V3 as the refining LLM on top of a fine-tuned 32B generator, so part of the gain reflects a much stronger model being applied, complicating attribution to the verification mechanism itself versus simply using a better backbone in the refinement loop.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated observation: user-oriented (PIE-style) optimization pairs are confined to a single programmer's incremental refinements, while a problem-oriented re-pairing captures cross-user algorithmic diversity. The multi-dimensional analysis (CFG edit distance, semantic embedding visualization, and human/GPT-4 categorization of global vs. local optimizations) convincingly characterizes the structural difference between the two datasets.

Extensive and consistent empirical evidence: fine-tuning experiments across five model families/scales (CodeLlama 13B, DeepSeek-Coder 7B/33B, Qwen2.5-Coder 7B/32B) all show large improvements from PCO over PIE (e.g., %OPT 31.24%→58.89%, SPEEDUP 2.95×→5.22×), which strengthens the claim beyond a single-model anecdote.

The anchor verification mechanism is a neat, domain-appropriate idea: exploiting the slow code as a functionally-correct oracle to label LLM-generated test inputs avoids the error-prone synthetic-label problem in code-generation test generation, and it outperforms self-debugging and direct test generation across three LLM backbones.

Useful supplementary analyses: data-efficiency study (30% of PCO exceeds full PIE), the %OPT/CORRECT gap analysis identifying correctness as the bottleneck, and detailed case studies illustrating both dataset-construction differences and failure modes of optimized code.
Reproducibility artifacts are reasonably documented: hardware, LoRA configuration, prompts, dataset statistics, and problem-level train/val/test splits are provided, with code publicly released.
weaknesses: Potential dataset-construction confound: PCO pairs are formed by ranking all cross-user submissions by runtime and retaining the same number of pairs per problem as PIE 'selecting those with the top speedup rankings'. This selection procedure biases PCO toward larger, easier speedup gains and changes the pair distribution beyond the mere 'problem-oriented' perspective, so the headline gains (31.24%→58.89%) may partly reflect this bias rather than the perspective shift alone. A control using randomly sampled cross-user pairs is needed.

The problem-oriented construction is conceptually simple — essentially re-pairing submissions across users by runtime order — and the paper could be critiqued as a dataset re-engineering exercise rather than a new method; the novelty is moderate for a top-tier venue.

Anchor verification is incremental relative to existing test-based validation work (CodeT, self-debugging, CodeT-style bidirectional filtering); the main difference is using the slow code as the label oracle, and the evaluation uses only 3 generated test inputs and a single refinement iteration, which may understate or misrepresent both the method and the baselines.

Scalability and applicability of the anchor oracle are not analyzed: executing very slow programs to label test inputs can be prohibitively expensive (the very programs most needing optimization), and the mechanism assumes the slow code is correct — unclear how often this fails or what the cost/time overhead is.

Best-of-k selection is potentially leaky: 'best refers to the fastest program that passes all test cases' does not specify whether selection uses ground-truth test cases or the verified anchor cases; using ground-truth tests would inflate BEST@8 results and complicate comparison with the prompting baselines.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only competitive-programming C++ code from CodeNet, timed in a gem5 simulator; no results on real-world or repository-level code where 'problem-oriented' diversity assumptions may not hold. Correctness is also defined against a limited test suite.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'first to introduce a problem-oriented perspective' is a somewhat thin novelty claim given related data-augmentation work in code optimization; the writing contains grammatical errors and loose phrasing (e.g., 'the research of LLMs to code optimization', 'integrate the diverse strategies and algorithm').

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: shifting from user-oriented (PIE-style) optimization pairs to problem-oriented pairs that aggregate solutions from multiple programmers, with a simple scaling analysis showing an order-of-magnitude increase in available pairs.

The 'optimization tax' observation (efficiency gains often come at the cost of correctness) is a genuine and practically relevant insight, and the anchor verification framework is an elegant solution that exploits the unique property of the optimization setting: the original slow code is functionally correct and can serve as a test oracle.

Comprehensive and careful experimental design: multiple model families and scales (CodeLlama, DeepSeekCoder, Qwen2.5-Coder, GPT-4/4o, DeepSeek-V3), instruction/CoT vs. fine-tuning comparisons, and a proper controlled ablation (PIE vs. PCO-Random vs. PCO-Top-Speedup in Appendix H) that disentangles the perspective effect from selection bias.

Thorough multi-dimensional analysis (structural GED analysis, semantic embedding analysis, human/LLM categorization of optimization types, GED-stratified training ablation, PCO percentage analysis), which substantiates the claim that problem-oriented pairs contain more global algorithmic changes.

Good validation beyond the main setup: Python replication, physical-hardware validation with correlation analysis against gem5, root-cause analysis of the anchor verification gains (Table 3), iteration count ablation, cost analysis, and failure mode analysis. Reproducibility details (training config, prompts, hardware) are well documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate. The problem-oriented perspective is essentially re-pairing existing submissions by runtime rather than by author, and the anchor verification framework is a relatively straightforward application of execution-based test generation (generate inputs, obtain outputs by executing a trusted program), closely related to existing test-feedback pipelines in code generation.

Evaluation rests on a small test set (41 problems, 978 pairs) inherited from PIE, which limits statistical reliability; no significance tests or variance estimates are reported, and the breadth of benchmarks is limited despite the scale of the claims.

The anchor verification framework requires that the 'slow' code be correct and executable, but the paper does not quantify how often this assumption fails in practice (e.g., TLE-prone original solutions whose execution is infeasible, or originals that are themselves buggy) and how the framework degrades in those cases; only qualitative mitigation strategies are proposed in Appendix L.

Some headline comparisons mix components: the strongest results combine PCO fine-tuning with test-generation-based refinement, making it harder to isolate how much of the end-to-end gain would transfer to settings without fine-tuned models; also, test-case generation quality is not analyzed (e.g., coverage or false-positive rates of anchor-verified tests).

Clarity issues: some sections read as promotional (repeated claims of 'significantly' improving), the Correct metric for anchor-verification-refined code could interact with the very test cases used for refinement, and a few results (e.g., Figures 2-3) are presented with limited statistical depth.

strengths: The paper is well-organized and easy to follow, with a clear two-part contribution structure (problem-oriented pair construction + anchor verification framework).

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: multi-dimensional dataset analysis (graph edit distance, embeddings, human/LLM categorization), a controlled ablation disentangling perspective from selection effects (Appendix H), Python cross-language replication, physical hardware validation of gem5 results, iteration-count sweeps, cost-benefit analysis of Best@k, and failure-mode analysis.

The anchor verification idea is sensible and well-motivated: exploiting the guaranteed correctness of the (slow) input program as an execution oracle to produce verified test cases is a clean insight specific to the optimization setting, and the root-cause comparison group (Table 3) isolates the source of the gains.
Reproducibility is supported by detailed prompts, training configurations, GPU-hour reporting, and dataset statistics in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core contributions. The 'problem-oriented' perspective amounts to sorting all submissions for a problem by runtime and pairing across users — a straightforward data-construction heuristic rather than a new method or insight. The anchor verification framework is essentially the well-known test-generation-with-execution-feedback loop (CodeT, etc.) with the slow code substituted as the oracle; this is a modest twist on established techniques.

A serious confound: pairs formed across different users are often independently developed solutions to the same problem, not true 'optimizations' of a given program. Fine-tuning on PCO may therefore teach the model to 're-solve the problem efficiently' (or even exploit problem-id-specific patterns) rather than to optimize given code. The paper's analysis (GED, embeddings) does not rule out this shortcut-learning interpretation, and no experiment (e.g., evaluating on truly unseen problems with held-out algorithmic families) directly addresses it.

The test set is very small: 41 unique problems and 978 pairs. Given this scale, differences like 58.90% vs. 61.55% correctness or per-metric gains in Table 2 could be sensitive to a handful of problems; no statistical significance testing or variance analysis across runs is provided.

Potential data contamination / train-test leakage concerns from building on CodeNet competitive-programming data are mentioned only briefly (problem-id disjointness) and not analyzed more deeply (e.g., near-duplicate problems across splits).

Baselines for the anchor verification comparison are somewhat weak or strawman-like: Self-Debugging with line-by-line explanation of an already-correct program is not a competitive correctness-repair baseline, and only 3 test inputs per problem are generated with a maximum of 1 refinement iteration in the main experiments, limiting the strength of the headline claims.

The 'optimization tax' phenomenon is framed as a key discovery but is essentially the well-understood fact that aggressive optimization can introduce semantic errors; the framing oversells a trivial observation.
Runtime measurements rely primarily on the gem5 simulator; hardware validation covers only 20 randomly selected pairs, which is thin support for real-world claims.

Writing issues persist: heavy use of vague intensity language ('new levels', 'significantly enhances ... to new levels'), and several claims (e.g., the scaling-law style pair-count argument in Section 2.1) are illustrative rather than rigorously established.

strengths: The problem-oriented perspective is a simple but well-motivated reframing of optimization pair construction, and the paper supports it with a multi-dimensional analysis (graph edit distance, semantic embeddings, human and LLM-based categorization of optimization types) rather than just asserting diversity gains.

The controlled ablation in Appendix H (PIE vs. PCO-Random vs. PCO-Top-Speedup with matched pair counts and hyperparameters) properly disentangles the perspective effect from the selection effect, addressing the most obvious confound in the main comparison.

The anchor verification idea is well-grounded in the structure of the task: the 'slow but correct' code provides a free, trusted oracle for test-case outputs, and Table 3 (comparison group generating outputs from the LLM instead of executing the slow code) convincingly isolates the source of the gains.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: multiple backbones (open and closed), BEST@k cost-benefit analysis, iteration-count ablation, GED-stratified training subsets, Python generalization, physical hardware validation of gem5 speedups (Pearson r=0.89), and systematic failure-mode analysis.
The 'optimization tax' observation (correctness-efficiency trade-off) is a genuine and useful empirical finding, and the paper is honest that anchor verification reduces but does not eliminate it.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate. The problem-oriented dataset is obtained by re-sorting existing PIE submissions by runtime across users, and anchor verification is a natural adaptation of execution-feedback refinement (CodeT, self-debugging, CoderEvolve-style loops) with the slow code as oracle. Both contributions are engineering-scale insights rather than conceptual advances, and the paper's framing ('first to introduce', 'to new levels') overstates the conceptual depth.

The test set is very small (978 pairs over only 41 problems, same split as PIE), so headline numbers like %OPT and SPEEDUP have substantial variance across problems; no per-problem variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported despite claims of 'significant' improvements.

Anchor verification uses only three LLM-generated test inputs per problem. This is a thin oracle; the remaining 53% 'compiled but semantically wrong' failure mode (Table 7) partly reflects this, and the paper does not analyze test-input coverage or compare against stronger verification (e.g., property-based or differential testing, more inputs).

Comparisons to the broader iterative-refinement literature are limited: only self-debugging and direct test generation are benchmarked; no comparison with reflection-style methods or prior optimization-specific pipelines, so the relative positioning of anchor verification is not fully established.

Potential distributional confound: PCO top-speedup pairs are selected using runtime measurements, and evaluation is on runtime; while PCO-Random mitigates this, the top-speedup selection could still bias the model toward outputs that are faster on the (small) test distribution rather than genuinely better optimizers.

Some writing issues: heavy reliance on bolded marketing-style claims, an unusually long appendix carrying core analyses (e.g., the perspective/selection disentanglement arguably belongs in the main text), and Figure 5-style results referenced with limited statistical detail.
Reproducibility of the closed-model experiments (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3 as refinement backbones) is inherently limited, and no code/data release is explicitly promised in the visible text.
